title: The Common Cold in Children
hook: Young kids catch a lot of colds — that's normal. Colds are viral, so antibiotics won't help; comfort care does, and OTC cough-and-cold medicines aren't safe for little ones.
key_points: Colds are caused by viruses, so antibiotics don't help — they only treat bacteria.
Supportive care is the treatment: extra rest, plenty of fluids, saline nose drops, and a humidifier.
Don't give over-the-counter cough or cold medicines to children under 4 — risk of dangerous side effects.
Call the doctor for trouble breathing, an earache, a fever beyond a few days, or any fever in a baby under 3 months.
content_html: If it feels like your young child is always coming down with something, that's actually expected — little ones catch many colds a year as their immune systems meet new viruses, especially in childcare. And because colds are caused by viruses, antibiotics don't help; the American Academy of Pediatrics notes antibiotics only fight bacteria and have no effect on the viruses behind colds and flu.
extra_html: There's no cure for a cold, so the goal is comfort while the body does its work: extra rest, plenty of fluids, saline (salt water) nose drops, and a humidifier to ease congestion. (Honey can help a cough — but only for children over one year, never younger.) Importantly, the AAP says over-the-counter cough and cold medicines should NOT be given to children under 4 because of the risk of dangerous side effects. Call your doctor if your child has trouble breathing, an earache, a fever that lasts beyond a few days or returns, or — at any time — if a baby under three months has a fever. This is general educational information; check with your pediatrician about your child.

related.title: When to Call the Doctor — Red Flags
related.hook: Most childhood illnesses are mild, but a handful of signs mean don't wait and watch — get medical help right away. Knowing them takes the guesswork out of a scary moment.

related.title: Fever Basics for Parents
related.hook: A fever is a sign the body is fighting infection, not a disease itself — how your child looks and acts often matters more than the exact number on the thermometer.

flashcards.prompt: Why don't antibiotics help with a common cold?

choices.text: Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics only treat bacteria
The dose for children is too small to work
Antibiotics work, but only after a week of symptoms

flashcards.explanation_html: Colds are viral infections. Antibiotics have no effect on viruses — they only fight bacteria — so they won't cure a cold.

flashcards.prompt: Should you give an over-the-counter cough or cold medicine to a 2-year-old?
flashcards.back_html: No. The AAP says OTC cough and cold medicines should not be given to children under 4 years because of the risk of dangerous side effects. Use comfort care instead.

flashcards.prompt: What's the right approach to caring for a child's cold?

choices.text: Supportive care — extra rest, fluids, saline drops, a humidifier
A course of antibiotics to clear it faster
Withholding fluids until the runny nose stops

flashcards.explanation_html: Colds have no cure, so the focus is comfort: rest, fluids, saline nose drops, and a humidifier to ease congestion while the body fights the virus.
